titre: The first American patent, for a potash recipe
accroche: On July 31, 1790, Washington signs the first American patent. It protects a potash recipe, not a spectacular invention.
contenu_vulgarise:
On July 31, 1790, in New York, then the federal capital of the United States, President George Washington signs a document with no precedent in the country's history: the first patent ever issued by the American government. The beneficiary is neither a gunsmith nor the inventor of a steam engine, but Samuel Hopkins, of the city of Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, who has just perfected a potash furnace.

Potash, and the pearl ash it allows one to produce, is used to make soap, glass, and fertilizer — uses as widespread as they were unspectacular for the time. The patent's own text describes the protected technical step: burning the raw ashes in a furnace before dissolving and boiling them in water, one extra step that leaves less residue and increases the yield of usable salt.

## A board of three, not a bureau

The federal patent law, passed on April 10, 1790, creates no specialized bureau: it entrusts the examination of each application to three members of Washington's cabinet — Secretary of State Thomas Jefferson, Secretary of War Henry Knox, and Attorney General Edmund Randolph. The three must judge the invention sufficiently useful and important before the president seals the document with his own signature. Hopkins thereby obtains, for fourteen years, the exclusive right to use and sell his process.

The system does not survive three years. As early as 1793, Congress radically simplifies the procedure: issuing a patent becomes a simple registration, entrusted to the Secretary of State alone, with no substantive examination. It would take until 1836 for a permanent office, staffed with technical examiners, to resume verifying applications.

## A furnace recipe, not a revolution

Nothing about this first patent resembles the image one likes to imagine: no spectacular invention, no founding stroke of genius. It is a process improvement in an already old chemical industry, granted to a craftsman whose very name eventually became blurred. Even today, govinfo.gov, the official publishing portal of the American government, names the beneficiary as “Samuel Hopkins, of Vermont.” The original document, however, leaves no room for doubt: it names Samuel Hopkins, of the city of Philadelphia and the State of Pennsylvania.

Most patents issued in those same years were not so fortunate as to be read and copied so often. A fire destroys the Patent Office on December 15, 1836, carrying away the records of nearly ten thousand patents granted since 1790.

repere.texte: Fourteen years: the length of the monopoly the first American patent grants its holder, on July 31, 1790.
repere.source: United States Patent No. X1, July 31, 1790 (Wikisource transcription)

carte.punch: The first American patent protects a potash furnace recipe, not an invention.
carte.idee: On July 31, 1790, Washington signs the very first United States patent: a potash-making process, granted to Samuel Hopkins for fourteen years. An American government portal still places its author in Vermont today; the original document, however, names him as being from Philadelphia.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: Covers the roughly ten thousand patents issued between 1790 and 1836, which at the time were identified only by title and date; the current sequential numbering only began in July 1836, and these earlier patents have since been catalogued by the office under the name “X-Patents.”

quiz.question: Why was Samuel Hopkins's patent not examined by a patent office?
choix: Because the inventor had waived any review of the content of his application
Because the 1790 law entrusted the examination to three cabinet members, before a permanent office was created in 1836
Because potash fell into no patentable category recognized by the law
Because the patent had been issued directly by Congress, with no involvement from the president
quiz.explication: The Patent Act of 1790 entrusts the examination to Jefferson, Knox, and Randolph; no permanent office exists before the 1836 reform, which creates the first technical examiners.
